extracted.intended_audience: government contracting officers, procurement lawyers, and agency legal staff dealing with federal contracts
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing when public advertising/competition is required for United States government contracts, and what changes may be made to existing contracts by supplemental agreement. Covers exceptions for useless competition, inter-departmental transfers, permissive informal agreements, and limits on supplemental contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition useless — no advertising required
rubrics_metrics.description: Where competition would be useless, advertising is not necessary (e.g., where there is no real competition for the required supply or service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: purchase of electric power where there was no real competition (C.18169, June 16, 1905); contracts where bidders possess proprietary information or methods (wireless telegraph stations in Alaska — O.12705, May 31, 1902); sales to licensors when original contract limited disposition to destruction or sale to licensor (C.20523, Oct. 17, 1906); leases to take sand and gravel where competition would be useless (O.17642, Mar. 8, 1905). The rule is applied where factual circumstances make solicitation of bids pointless or impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability to secure competition — advertising dispensed
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is impracticable to secure competition (e.g., rare/difficult-to-obtain items), advertising may be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Army War College seeking many rare maps where bidders could not determine cost — advertising dispensed under act of Mar. 2, 1903 (C.16018, Mar. 12, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative adoption of plan precludes competitive advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress appropriates for alteration of a particular monument based on a report referring to a specific plan approved by interested parties, legislative adoption of that plan implies it cannot be materially departed from and competition may be useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a private company has exclusive right to use the adopted plans, competition is useless and advertising can be excepted (C.19834, May 24, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory language 'by contract or otherwise' can permit non-advertised methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statute authorizes execution 'by contract or otherwise' within cost limits and approved plans, work may be performed under alternative arrangements (e.g., percentage plan) without advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Act of March 3, 1905 for West Point improvements permitted construction on percentage plan and without advertisement (G.20947, Jan. 18, 1907 & Feb. 3, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Once-duly-advertised satisfies the law (single advertisement suffices)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, pursuant to section 3709, an advertisement has been once duly made, the law has been complied with; repeat advertisement is not strictly necessary though permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If advertisement yields no results, contracting officers may resort to open-market purchase without further advertising in certain circumstances; but open-market purchases must be limited to the article(s) previously advertised in some cases (C.313, Oct. 5, 1894; C.20298, Aug. 28, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-market purchases allowed after unsuccessful advertisement (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposals invited produce no acceptable bids (or are unreasonable), an open-market purchase without advertising may be made, but is often limited to the article(s) previously advertised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Par. 559 A.E. 1910 describes open-market purchase authorization; cases show limitation that purchases be limited to items previously advertised (C.313, Oct. 5, 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-departmental transfers at cost rely on original advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: One department may lawfully obtain articles from another at cost price on the theory that the original purchase complied with advertising and contracting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: National Soldiers' Home purchasing clothing from Quartermaster's Department if deemed more suitable than that obtained by contracts (C.26911, June 20, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal agreements may be used for certain services instead of formal contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: In some contexts (e.g., services provided by institutions under local control), informal agreements without advertisement are proper rather than formal contracts under section 3744, R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Agreement with San Lazaro Hospital, Manila, for care of insane Filipino soldiers — held to be by informal agreement without advertising (C.23229, Aug. 4, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-exchange and instrumentalities may contract without advertising (but not compete unfairly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations of a post exchange (an instrumentality of the U.S.) may do internal work (e.g., laundry) without advertisement; but the post exchange, being exempt from commercial burdens, should not compete with others for public supplies or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: post hospital contracting with post-exchange laundry (O.18156, Oct. 31, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract requires a live executory contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the Secretary can close out a contract by a compromise (supplemental) agreement there must be a live executory contract in existence to close out; if the contract has been canceled and annulled, supplemental settlement authority does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a contract still exists as executory (even if one party performed completely), a supplemental contract may be used to compromise damages; but where contract actually canceled/annulled, rights are fixed and cannot be settled by supplemental contract (C.3969, Oct. 11, 1898; C.10502, May 16, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract not necessary for time extensions when contract permits officer determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract provides that the contractor may be allowed additional time as the constructing officer may determine, a supplemental contract is not necessary; written notice of the determination suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: C.17597, Feb. 27, 1905 — notify contractor in writing of determination of additional time rather than entering supplemental contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract confined to modification of the original specific undertaking
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental contract must be confined to modification merely of the specific undertaking which is the subject of the original contract; it cannot introduce new and distinct work or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A modification that introduces any new matter not originally contracted for (different and distinct work or service) is a new and independent contract requiring prior advertisement and is not legitimate as a supplemental contract (cases: dredging locality changes, substitution of marble for sandstone — e.g., P.64,344 Apr.12,1894; Schneider v. U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts cannot add quantities beyond original advertisement limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the contract contains a provision allowing increases, parties cannot, by mutual agreement, permit delivery of quantities not called for in the original advertisement; additional quantity beyond the advertised scope requires new advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Advertisement for quartermaster stores with a provision allowing increase during fiscal year did not authorize delivery of quantity not called for — additional stores must be obtained after advertisement as required by law (R.37, 478, Apr. 18, 1876). Also where advertised amount had cap (e.g., increase not to exceed 50%), contracts covering amounts beyond that cap require fresh advertisement (C.25979, Dec. 23, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract cannot be used to cover work materially different in locality or character
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental contract substituting work at a different locality or of materially different character than advertised is illegal and constitutes a new contract requiring advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: substituting Ingomar for Barnes Landing (different locality) — supplemental contract illegal (O.475, Oct. 18, 1894); substituting dredging of fine hard sand from outer bar when original called for hard pan, boulders, soft mud — supplemental contract illegal (C.1454, June 18, 1895); additional width dredging after original completed not a modification (C.8658, July 26, 1900).

rubrics_metrics.name: New/unforeseen distinct work developed during performance requires new advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: If during execution a quite new and distinct work develops that was not embraced in the original contract (e.g., removal of a bar formed after commencement), such work cannot be included by consent in the existing contract or covered by supplemental contract without advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: removal of a bar formed after contract began — must have new advertisement and a separate formal contract (P.47,257, May 20, 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts may be used for necessary adjustments that are not prejudicial to Government interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental contracts can properly cover additional expenditures or changes that arise from site conditions, unforeseen needed work, or adjustments that do not prejudice the interests of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible examples listed: additional masonry due to site; extra excavation in cofferdam foundations; substitute pile lengths; including rock excavation when only common excavation specified; depositing dredged material on private ground; working additional shifts; vesting title on partial payments; purchase of mineral oil with lower flash test at reduced price; increased fill due to subsidence; payment in full for individual buildings by supplemental contract; annulling original contract and reimbursing contractor; adding sliding supports for drawers; compensation for additional time due to government-caused delay (many cited cases: C.2700; C.2927; C.6244; C.3423; C.9085; C.9410; C.26846; C.24531; C.1825; C.19861; C.13401; O.23546; etc.). The common theme: changes must be within scope of modification and not against Government interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contracts cannot settle unliquidated breach claims against the Government
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental contract cannot be used to settle unliquidated claims against the United States arising from a breach of the contract; such claims must be liquidated by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court limited the power to settle unliquidated claims in Cramp & Sons v. U.S., 216 U.S. 503; see XVII Comp. Dec. 806, 810.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to abandon or modify contracts for exclusive Government benefit may justify supplemental settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it becomes necessary for the exclusive benefit of the Government to abandon work under a contract, a supplemental contract providing for agreed damages or settlement (fixed lump sum) and approved by the Secretary may authorize payment to the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: XV Comp. Dec. 439 — supplemental contract entered into and approved by Secretary of War to fix contractor's damages allowed payment; contractor's profit and loss from abandonment can be proper elements of damage. Other examples permit annulling original contract when conditions change materially (G.5195, Oct. 21, 1898).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for completion may be extended where Government interests not prejudiced
rubrics_metrics.description: Under prior precedent, the time for completion of a contract may be extended to a future specified date provided the Government interests will not be prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: II Comp. Dec. 242, 635; various other Comp. Decs.; rule from 91 U.S. 322 applied.
